fields.sections.1.exchanges.1.pro.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle raises a legitimate semantic caution that ebed ranges beyond chattel slavery, so meaning must be determined within each disputed legal context. Principal limitation: His unsourced six-percent and 93-or-94-percent breakdown has an unclear denominator and categories, never specifies whether the figures concern Hebrew ebed, Greek doulos, or both, leaves “servitude” undefined, and obscures its conclusion through phrases like “hanging too tightly” and “all of the issues”. Live burden: To advance the regulation defense, he must classify relevant occurrences and explain why acquisition, inheritance, permanence, and differential-treatment language in Leviticus and Exodus supports morally defensible service rather than the ownership institution alleged by Bowen and Dillahunty. Locked score: 64 fits a relevant, charitable contextual question whose imprecise statistical framing and absence of passage-level analysis materially limit its evidential force.
